echoes.note: The Judean teachers demand circumcision 'after the custom of Moses' as necessary for salvation; the underlying institution is the Abrahamic covenant of circumcision, the sign required of every male, where the uncircumcised is 'cut off.' The whole dispute presupposes this text as the charter of the boundary marker. Verbal coherence ('circumcised') and thematic centrality are strong.

The Mosaic codification of circumcision (eighth-day) is what 'the custom of Moses' (v.1) most directly names, distinguishing the demand here from the merely Abrahamic command; supports the phrase 'keep the law of Moses' (v.5).

The Torah's own rule that a foreigner must be circumcised before sharing in the Passover/community is the legal logic the circumcision party extends to Gentile believers — only the circumcised may belong. Faint, conceptual.

Peter calls God the one 'who knows the heart' (kardiognostes, v.8) who 'made no distinction... cleansing their hearts.' This recalls the LORD who, unlike man looking on outward appearance, 'looks on the heart' — here applied to overturning the outward circumcision marker in favor of inward purity. Strong thematic coherence.

Solomon's prayer addresses God who alone 'knows the hearts of all the children of men'; a recurrent OT divine epithet standing behind Peter's heart-knowing God who reads Gentile faith. Recurrence test supports the motif.
'I the LORD search the heart' — part of the same cluster of heart-searching texts informing v.8's claim that God testified about the Gentiles by reading their hearts.

God 'cleansing their hearts by faith' (v.9) echoes the promise that the LORD will circumcise the heart — interiorized, divinely-wrought purity displacing the external rite at issue in the chapter. Thematically potent for the circumcision debate.

Heart-cleansing language (v.9) coheres with the promise to sprinkle clean water, give a new heart, and put the Spirit within — note v.8's gift of the Spirit alongside the cleansing. The Spirit + cleansed heart pairing is striking.
'Circumcise the foreskin of your heart' reinforces the inward-circumcision motif behind 'cleansing their hearts' (v.9). Faint, overlaps with Deut 30:6.

Peter's 'yoke... which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear' (v.10) uses yoke-as-burden imagery; OT yoke metaphor (e.g., the good of bearing the yoke) lies in the background, though Peter inverts it as an unbearable load. Figural/contested.

James's formal scriptural proof (vv.16-17): 'I will... build the tabernacle of David which has fallen... that the rest of men may seek after the Lord, all the Gentiles who are called by my name.' This follows the Septuagint against the Hebrew: MT 'that they may possess the remnant of Edom' becomes LXX 'that the rest of mankind may seek' (Heb. yireshu 'possess' read as yidreshu 'seek'; 'Edom' read as 'adam, mankind) — the very reading that makes Gentile inclusion the prophetic point. Highest volume and decisive function in the argument.

The opening of the citation, 'After these things I will return' (v.16), is not in Amos; it most closely matches 'I will return and have compassion on them,' suggesting James has conflated Amos with Jeremiah's restoration promise. A genuine secondary source spliced into the quotation.

'Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God and David their king' shares the post-restoration 'seek the Lord' + Davidic motif underlying vv.16-17. Possible contributor to the catena's 'after these things... seek the Lord.' Contested.

James says God 'first visited the nations, to take out of them a people for his name' (v.14). The phrase 'a people for his name/possession' reuses the election formula by which Israel was 'a people for his own possession' — now extended to Gentiles. Strong thematic reuse of covenant election language.

'A people for his name' (v.14) echoes the Sinai promise that Israel would be God's 'treasured possession out of all peoples' — the foundational election text now applied to the nations. Recurrence with Deut 7:6 / 14:2.

'Many nations shall join themselves to the LORD in that day and shall be my people' anticipates God taking a people from the Gentiles (v.14); part of the prophetic stream James invokes ('the words of the prophets,' v.15). Faint.

The closing tag, 'known to him from eternity / who declared these things of old' (vv.17b-18), resembles Isaiah's 'Who has declared this from of old?' — supplying the 'long-known to God' coloring appended to the Amos citation. Contested wording.

James's first prohibition, 'the pollution of idols' (v.20), corresponds to the resident-alien (ger) law forbidding sacrifices offered apart from the LORD — i.e., meat from idol-worship. The four-item decree as a whole derives from the laws binding on the stranger sojourning in Israel (Lev 17-18). High coherence; foundational to the decree.

The prohibition of 'blood' (v.20) directly reuses the repeated Levitical ban applying to both Israelite and the resident alien: 'no one of you shall eat blood.' Explicitly extended to the ger, which is why it grounds rules for Gentile believers.

'What is strangled' (v.20) reflects the requirement to drain the blood of any animal caught/killed — flesh with blood in it (a strangled animal) is forbidden, again binding on the sojourner. The 'strangled'/blood pairing in the decree mirrors this law.

'Sexual immorality' (porneia, v.20) corresponds to the forbidden-unions catalogue of Lev 18, which v.26 expressly imposes on 'the stranger that sojourns among you.' The decree's fourth item completes the set of Holiness-Code rules for resident aliens.

The blood prohibition (v.20) also rests on the Noahic command given to all humanity — 'flesh with its life, its blood, you shall not eat' — which suits Gentiles since it precedes and exceeds Israel's law. Often paired with Lev 17 as the rationale for a universally-binding minimum.
'Moses... read in the synagogues every Sabbath' (v.21) presupposes the Sabbath institution as the appointed day of holy convocation. Faint, institutional background to the verse.

The written decree restates the prohibitions: 'things sacrificed to idols' (v.29) reuses the Levitical ban on sacrifices offered outside the LORD's worship, binding on the resident alien. Repetition of the v.20 list.
'Blood' (v.29) again reflects the Holiness Code's repeated prohibition extended to the sojourner.
'Things strangled' (v.29) reflects the requirement to drain blood from killed animals; flesh retaining blood is forbidden to Israelite and stranger alike.
'Sexual immorality' (v.29) corresponds to the forbidden unions of Lev 18, imposed on the resident alien (v.26). The letter's four items reproduce the ger-laws of Lev 17-18.
The blood abstention (v.29) coheres with the universal Noahic command against eating flesh with its blood, the natural basis for a rule binding on Gentiles.
